title: Part II — TOPOLOGY: Teams and Their Interfaces

know: Part II answers three questions in order: which kinds of teams an organization needs, how they should work with each other, and how large they should be.
can_do: Pick the Part II chapter that answers the question in front of them.

audience.who: Executives and individual contributors in product and tech who have read Part I and are about to start Part II, or who arrive with one question about teams and want the chapter that answers it.
already_knows: How software teams work day to day.
Part I's rules: size what a team owns by its cognitive load, place boundaries on fracture planes, find the constraint before adding capacity.
Corvane in outline, and the Launch Queue of 2024: eleven product teams, a platform team of five, lead time from 4 days to 19.
does_not_know: Stream-aligned, platform, enabling and complicated-subsystem team as defined types (chapter 6); glossed in a clause each here.
Collaboration, X-as-a-Service and facilitating as interaction modes, and the team API (chapter 7); glossed here.
Where the six-to-eight rule of thumb comes from (chapter 8).

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of this page alone can name the three chapters' subjects in reading order.
acceptance_criteria.probe: After reading only this page: what will each of the next three chapters tell you, in order?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Team types; interaction modes and team APIs; team size and composition.

thesis.question: Which kinds of teams does an organization need, how should they work with each other, and how large should they be?
thesis.claim: An organization needs four team types — stream-aligned teams, and the platform, enabling and complicated-subsystem teams that exist to serve them — and three interaction modes — collaboration, X-as-a-Service and facilitating — chosen so that the teams aligned to a flow of user value carry the least load and wait the least; team size follows from the load the team must carry, the on-call rotation it must sustain and the cost of its internal coordination, and each of these choices is written down as a contract others can read.
thesis.disputed_by: The practice of organizing by function or technology (front end, back end, QA, operations) with teams sized by budget, and the view that naming team types is a consultant's vocabulary laid over the same org chart.
thesis.so_what: A leader can test every team in the organization with two questions — whose load does it lower, and whose waiting does it remove — and can refuse a new team or a new dependency that answers neither.
thesis.how_why: Part I showed that a team can own only what it understands and that output is set by the slowest step. Teams aligned to a stream of user value are where value is produced, so every other team is justified by what it takes off them; interactions are where waiting arises, so they are limited and made explicit; and size is bounded below by what a rotation and a manager need and above by what a group can coordinate.

supporting_claims.claim: Four team types are enough, and each of the three that are not stream-aligned is justified by the load it removes from stream-aligned teams or the waiting it prevents; a team that does neither is overhead.
Two teams should work in one of three modes, chosen deliberately and written down as a team API, because an unchosen interaction turns into a queue or a standing meeting.

Team size is derived from the load the team carries, the on-call rotation it must sustain and its internal coordination cost; the familiar six-to-eight is the result of that derivation under stated assumptions, and it changes when the assumptions do.

role.contribution: Performs the part's opening: states the part thesis and the reading order.

additional_patterns.applies_to: three-choices and the chapter list in the closing: type, then mode, then size

flow.rationale: The page opens on a helping team that became the place where work waited, and on the two questions nobody had answered about it. The first section then gives the test that Part I's rules supply for any team; the second applies the test three times, to the type of a team, to the way two teams work together and to a team's size, and ends by saying why the three come in that order; the chapter list closes the page. The test stands before the three choices because each choice is justified by it; put the choices first and the four types and three modes arrive as a vocabulary with no reason behind it. The list comes last because a reader can choose a chapter only after seeing what each decides.

hook.content: Corvane's platform team of five was created to help eleven product teams release faster, and within a year it was the place where every launch waited.

bridge.from_reader_world: The reader's experience of a team set up to help other teams that became the place where their work waits.
bridge.to_topic: The two questions that experience raises and that the usual explanations (too few people, too slow) skip: what kind of team it was meant to be, and how the other teams were meant to use it.

thesis_statement.text: Part II argues that an organization needs four team types and three ways for two teams to work together, chosen so that the teams that deliver to users carry the least load and wait the least, that team size follows from load, on-call duty and coordination cost, and that each choice is written down where others can read it.

promises.promise: The test Part I's rules give for any team: whose load it lowers and whose waiting it removes.
Three chapters answer three questions in order: which kinds of teams an organization needs, how they should work with each other, and how large they should be; and why the three come in that order.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Corvane's platform team of five was formed in 2022 so that product teams could release faster, and by 2024 it was the place where their launches waited.

evidence.what: Corvane (fictional): platform team of five formed in 2022, led by Lena Brandt; eleven product teams formed in 2023; in 2024, at 180 people, 14 launch requests open and a change that took about two days to write waiting about seventeen for a launch slot.
evidence.shows: A team created to remove waiting became the longest wait in the flow.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A helping team that becomes a bottleneck is usually explained by its staffing or its speed, and the questions that explain it are what kind of team it was meant to be and how the others were meant to use it, neither of which Corvane's 2022 plan answered.

evidence.what: Corvane's 2022 plan (fictional) gave the platform team a purpose (shared release tooling) and a headcount (five); it did not say what kind of team it was to be or how eleven teams were to use it.
evidence.source: _research/scenario-ledger.md (chapter 2 lines; the last clause is appended by this page)
evidence.shows: The two questions were open from the start, which is where the part begins.

transition_in.carries_over: The platform team that became the place where launches waited.
transition_in.introduces: The reader's own version of that team, and the two questions that explain it.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Part II argues that an organization needs four team types and three interaction modes chosen so that the teams delivering to users carry the least load and wait the least, with team size derived and each choice written down, and it makes the argument in three chapters that answer three questions in order.

transition_in.carries_over: The two unanswered questions about the platform team.
transition_in.introduces: The part's claim, which answers them for every team, and the three questions its chapters take in turn.

sections.heading: The Test: Whose Load, Whose Waiting
sections.controlling_idea: Teams aligned to a stream of user value are where value is produced, so every other team and every dependency is justified by what it does to their load and their waiting.

advances_thesis.how: States the principle from which the part derives its types, modes and sizes.

transition_in.carries_over: The part's claim as stated in the lead.
transition_in.introduces: The reasoning from Part I's rules that produces it, as a two-question test.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Part I's rules, that a team can own only what it understands and that output is set by the slowest step, give a test for every team and every dependency: whose load does it lower, and whose waiting does it remove.

evidence.what: Value is produced by the teams aligned to a stream of user value; load limits what they can own and waiting limits how fast their work arrives; anything else in the organization is justified by what it takes off them.
evidence.shows: Why two questions are enough to judge a team or a dependency.

sections.heading: Three Choices: Type, Mode and Size
sections.controlling_idea: The test is applied three times, to what a team is for, to how two teams work together and to how many people a team has, and the three choices depend on each other in that order.

advances_thesis.how: One paragraph per supporting claim, each naming the choice and its justification.

flow.rationale: A mode is chosen between two teams of known types, so types come first; size depends on what the team owns and on how much of its time its interactions take, so it comes third. The paragraph on the order closes the section because the dependency can be stated only once all three choices have been met; put size first, as Corvane's plan did, and it is a number with nothing to derive it from.

transition_in.introduces: The three choices it is applied to.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Four team types are enough: stream-aligned teams, and platform, enabling and complicated-subsystem teams that are each justified by what they take off stream-aligned teams.

advances_thesis.how: Names the four types with one clause each and the justification the three serving types share.

evidence.what: The four fundamental team types of Team Topologies (Skelton and Pais, 2019).
evidence.shows: The types are a named source's model, which chapter 6 presents and tests.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Two teams should work together in one of three modes (collaboration, X-as-a-Service or facilitating), chosen deliberately and written down as a team API, because an interaction nobody chose turns into a queue or a standing meeting.

advances_thesis.how: Names the three modes and the written contract, and the cost of leaving the choice unmade.

evidence.what: The three interaction modes and the team API of Team Topologies (Skelton and Pais, 2019).
evidence.shows: The modes are a named source's model, which chapter 7 presents.

transition_in.carries_over: Four team types and what each is for.
transition_in.introduces: How teams of those types work with each other, and how that is written down.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Team size is derived from the load the team carries, the on-call rotation it must sustain and the cost of its internal coordination, and the familiar six to eight is the result of that derivation under stated assumptions.

advances_thesis.how: States size as a derivation and the rule of thumb as its result.

evidence.what: Will Larson's rules of thumb in An Elegant Puzzle (2019): six to eight engineers per manager; about eight engineers for a two-tier on-call rotation.
evidence.shows: The number is one author's rule of thumb with reasons, which chapter 8 examines.

transition_in.carries_over: Types and modes, which decide what a team owns and how much of its time others take.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Types come first because a mode is chosen between two teams of known types, and size comes last because it depends on the team's type and on its interactions; a size chosen first is a number with nothing to derive it from.

evidence.what: Corvane's 2022 plan (fictional) fixed the platform team at five before saying what it would own or how eleven teams would reach it.
evidence.shows: Size chosen first, with nothing to derive it from.

transition_in.carries_over: The three choices: type, mode and size.
transition_in.introduces: The one direction in which they depend on each other, and what happens when size is chosen first.

advances_thesis.how: Shows the three supporting claims as steps that depend on each other.

conclusion.heading: Chapters in this part
conclusion.synthesis: The three chapters ask one question about a team from three sides: what it is for, how others reach it and how many people that takes. Asked of Corvane's platform team, they turn a staffing complaint into three separate design decisions.
conclusion.so_what: A reader can test every team in their organization with two questions, whose load it lowers and whose waiting it removes, and can refuse a new team or a new dependency that answers neither.

callback.to: Corvane's platform team of five from the opening (p01).
callback.how: The closing reads its 2022 plan against the three questions: the first two left unanswered, the third answered with a bare number.

takeaway.content: Read the chapters in order; with one question about a team in hand, open the chapter that answers it.

decision_log.decision: The post entry in the journal spec has a question and no thesis. Intent outcome, AC-1 and role are copied from the post entry; the hook from the part's opening.
rejected: Writing a separate thesis from the page's question.

decision_log.decision: The page ends with 'Chapters in this part' as its headed conclusion, with two units: the chapter list and one closing paragraph that holds the synthesis, the callback and the hand-off to chapter 6.
rejected: A separate 'Where to Begin' section after the list.

decision_log.decision: The three chapters of Part II were being written in parallel, so the page describes them from their journal-spec entries only and names no worked example of theirs.

decision_log.decision: The page does not give the part's closing verdict on the platform team (right type, wrong mode, too few people for its scope); it says only that the three decisions were not made. The verdict is chapter 8's to deliver.

decision_log.decision: Flow rubric (one fresh reader, order of ideas only): sound with notes. Taken: the one-paragraph section 'Why Types Come First and Size Last' is merged into 'Three Choices: Type, Mode and Size' as its closing paragraph (p08), because its idea repeated that section's own ordering; the closing no longer says 'none of the three had been answered', since the opening raises two questions and the plan did give a size: it now says the plan left the first two unanswered and answered the third with a bare number. 'Team API' is glossed where it first appears.
rejected: Reducing the chapter list to bare links or dropping the three questions from the lead: AC-1 needs the subjects in the lead, and the brief asks for one line per chapter with its question.
